down-payment-assistance.html.main_text: Down Payment Assistance for Eligible HomebuyersThere may be state, local, or lender programs for eligible buyers. Assistance can come with income limits, education requirements, repayment terms, and restrictions on the home or mortgage.Check the program before counting the fundsAsk a participating lender to confirm current availability and how the assistance works with your main loan. CalHFA’s MyHome is one California option to discuss, with eligibility and lender requirements.Understand the repaymentAssistance is not always a grant. A deferred payment loan may be due later under the program’s terms. Review what happens when you sell, refinance, or stop occupying the home.01Identify a programState, local, or lender option02Confirm eligibilityIncome, ownership history, and property03Review the termsAmount, repayment, and education04Coordinate approvalMain mortgage and assistance togetherCalifornia and San Fernando Valley contextFor a San Fernando Valley purchase, the lender determines eligibility and loan terms, while the property can add costs such as taxes, HOA dues, insurance, repairs, and appraisal related issues. Compare written lender disclosures with the full cost of the specific home.Understanding Assistance Terms Before ApplyingHomebuyer assistance is not always a grant. It may be a loan, a deferred repayment arrangement, or another form of help with conditions attached. Review whether the assistance must be repaid, whether a balance or other obligation grows, and what happens after a sale, refinance, transfer, or change in occupancy.Program availability and eligibility can change. A participating lender can identify the current requirements for your household, the property, and the first mortgage. Compare the complete financing arrangement, including future repayment obligations, rather than judging the program only by the help available at the time of purchase.Balancing a Down Payment With Remaining SavingsA down payment is one part of the funds needed to buy a home. Closing expenses, moving, immediate repairs, and a reserve for ordinary surprises can also affect the amount you want to contribute. The largest contribution you can assemble is not automatically the most comfortable choice if it leaves too little available afterward.Compare several eligible loan arrangements with a lender using the same property and assumptions. A different contribution can change mortgage insurance, the loan amount, and the overall payment. Review where each part of the purchase funds comes from and what documentation is needed before moving money or making a commitment.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesCalHFA, Homebuyer ProgramsYour Financing OptionsReview the financing resources and connect with a lender when you are ready.Connect With a Lender

down-payment-needed.html.main_text: Planning Your Down PaymentYour required down payment depends on the loan, the home, and your qualifications. Compare a few cash contributions, then include closing costs and the savings you want to keep after moving.Separate the down payment from other costsThe down payment reduces the amount borrowed. Closing costs, prepaid expenses, and your reserve funds are separate parts of the budget. Ask for a written estimate that shows each item.Review a down payment range for your home searchThe comparison below is arithmetic, not a promise that a program is available. A lender can identify which down payment choices fit your credit, income, and property.Illustrative purchase priceDown payment only. Closing costs and reserves are additional. Examples do not establish program eligibility.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor a San Fernando Valley purchase, the lender determines eligibility and loan terms, while the property can add costs such as taxes, HOA dues, insurance, repairs, and appraisal related issues. Compare written lender disclosures with the full cost of the specific home.Balancing a Down Payment With Remaining SavingsA down payment is one part of the funds needed to buy a home. Closing expenses, moving, immediate repairs, and a reserve for ordinary surprises can also affect the amount you want to contribute. The largest contribution you can assemble is not automatically the most comfortable choice if it leaves too little available afterward.Compare several eligible loan arrangements with a lender using the same property and assumptions. A different contribution can change mortgage insurance, the loan amount, and the overall payment. Review where each part of the purchase funds comes from and what documentation is needed before moving money or making a commitment.Understanding Written Loan TermsCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.Ask which conditions remain before approval and what changes require a new review. New debt, a change in employment or documented income, or a property issue can affect financing before closing. Use the lender’s current disclosures and explanations rather than relying on a general program description as a promise of eligibility or final terms.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesYour Financing OptionsReview the financing resources and connect with a lender when you are ready.Connect With a Lender

fha-loans.html.main_text: FHA Loans and Smaller Down PaymentsFHA insured mortgages can allow a smaller down payment for eligible buyers. Lender approval, mortgage insurance, and property requirements still apply, so compare the complete financing arrangement before selecting the program.Look at the fit, not just the down paymentCredit, income, debt, the property, and the lender’s requirements still matter. The allowable loan amount also depends on the county and property. A lender can confirm the requirements that apply to your purchase.Ask for comparable offersCompare an FHA offer with other options using the same price and down payment. Review the monthly payment, mortgage insurance, upfront costs, and how long you expect to keep the loan.3.5%Minimum down payment for eligible FHA borrowers01BorrowerCredit, income, and debt review02PropertyCondition and appraisal review03BudgetInsurance and closing costsCalifornia and San Fernando Valley contextFor a San Fernando Valley purchase, the lender determines eligibility and loan terms, while the property can add costs such as taxes, HOA dues, insurance, repairs, and appraisal related issues. Compare written lender disclosures with the full cost of the specific home.Understanding Written Loan TermsCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.Ask which conditions remain before approval and what changes require a new review. New debt, a change in employment or documented income, or a property issue can affect financing before closing. Use the lender’s current disclosures and explanations rather than relying on a general program description as a promise of eligibility or final terms.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesYour Financing OptionsReview the financing resources and connect with a lender when you are ready.Connect With a Lender

First TimeHomebuyersUnderstand the whole buying process, from preapproval and touring to your offer, negotiations, and closing.

First Time HomebuyersFirst Time HomebuyersFirst Time HomebuyersFirst Time HomebuyersFirst Time Homebuyers01Getting Preapproved for Your First HomeStart with a comfortable monthly payment and the money available for your purchase. A lender reviews your income, credit, debts, and savings so you can understand your financing options before choosing a home.Gather the requested documents and review what the preapproval includes. Use that information to set a search range that fits your budget, not simply the largest amount available.Read More02Touring Homes as a First Time BuyerWith a price range in place, narrow down the neighborhoods, home features, and timing that matter to you. Compare the listings with your priorities before deciding which homes to tour.At each showing, look beyond the photographs to the layout, condition, storage, and surrounding area. Keep notes so you can compare properties and decide which home fits your everyday life.Read More03Making an Offer on Your First HomeWhen you find a home you want to buy, put the price and the rest of the terms together. Review the financing, contingencies, deposit, and proposed timing before the offer is submitted.The offer page explains how these pieces work together so you can understand what you are proposing and which details matter to your purchase.Read More04Understanding Home Purchase NegotiationsThe seller may accept your offer, make a counteroffer, or decline it. Review the complete response, including changes to price, timing, credits, or other terms, before deciding how to respond.Keep your original priorities and limits in view, particularly when there are competing offers. The goal is an agreement you understand and are comfortable moving forward with.Read More05Closing on Your First HomeAfter an agreement is reached, follow the transaction deadlines for inspections, disclosures, financing, and closing documents. Review the property information and complete the final walkthrough before the purchase is finished.Once the transaction is complete and possession is available, you receive the keys. The closing page explains the work between an accepted offer and moving into your first home.Read MorePlan Your First Home PurchaseBuy With Dominique

first-time-closing.html.main_text: Closing on Your First HomeClosing is the final stage of buying a home, when the remaining contract and loan requirements are completed and ownership is transferred. Review the disclosures, signing instructions, final walkthrough, and agreed possession timing before treating the move as complete.ReviewStay on top of the documents, disclosures, and remaining transaction deadlines.InspectComplete the inspections and review the results so you understand the property before moving forward.Finalize FinancingProvide the lender with any remaining documents and confirm the loan is ready for closing.Final WalkthroughVisit the home again shortly before closing to confirm its condition and any agreed work.KeysOnce the transaction is complete and possession is available, the home becomes yours.Plan Your Home SearchBuy With DominiqueUnderstanding the Final TransferAn accepted offer is not the same as a completed purchase. Financing, title, disclosures, contract conditions, and signing requirements still need to be resolved before the home changes hands. Review the closing documents against the agreed terms and clarify any difference while there is time to address it.Possession should follow the written agreement, which may not match the moment documents are signed. Coordinate the final walkthrough, funds, keys, and moving arrangements with the professionals handling the transaction. Verify payment instructions independently through a known contact rather than acting on an unexpected message asking you to send money elsewhere.Understanding Written Loan TermsCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.Ask which conditions remain before approval and what changes require a new review. New debt, a change in employment or documented income, or a property issue can affect financing before closing. Use the lender’s current disclosures and explanations rather than relying on a general program description as a promise of eligibility or final terms.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan Estimates

first-time-homebuyer-programs.html.main_text: First Time Homebuyer Programs in CaliforniaFirst time homebuyer programs can reduce upfront costs or make financing more affordable for eligible buyers. A lender can confirm whether you qualify and which programs fit the home you want.Understanding Program EligibilityFirst time homebuyer programs can assist eligible buyers, but the meaning of first time buyer and the other requirements depend on the program. Review the current household, property, occupancy, education, and lender conditions before assuming a past ownership history makes you eligible or ineligible.California Homebuyer AssistanceCalHFA publishes information about its first mortgage and assistance programs. Some assistance is structured as a deferred repayment loan rather than a grant, so the repayment terms matter alongside the help available at purchase. A participating lender can explain which current options fit your application and property.Comparing the Complete Financing ArrangementEvaluate the first mortgage and any assistance together. Confirm how a sale, refinance, transfer, or change in use affects repayment. A program that lowers immediate cash needs can still create a future obligation, and availability or funding may change before you are ready to buy.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor a San Fernando Valley purchase, the lender determines eligibility and loan terms, while the property can add costs such as taxes, HOA dues, insurance, repairs, and appraisal related issues. Compare written lender disclosures with the full cost of the specific home.Understanding Assistance Terms Before ApplyingHomebuyer assistance is not always a grant. It may be a loan, a deferred repayment arrangement, or another form of help with conditions attached. Review whether the assistance must be repaid, whether a balance or other obligation grows, and what happens after a sale, refinance, transfer, or change in occupancy.Program availability and eligibility can change. A participating lender can identify the current requirements for your household, the property, and the first mortgage. Compare the complete financing arrangement, including future repayment obligations, rather than judging the program only by the help available at the time of purchase.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesCalHFA, Homebuyer ProgramsYour Financing OptionsReview the financing resources and connect with a lender when you are ready.Connect With a Lender

first-time-negotiations.html.main_text: Understanding Home Purchase NegotiationsHome purchase negotiations can change the price, contingencies, credits, repairs, and timing of a proposed sale. Review the complete written terms and their effect on your financing and protections before accepting a response.If the Offer Is AcceptedReview the next deadlines and make sure you understand what needs to happen immediately after acceptance.If the Seller CountersA counter can change price, timing, credits, or other terms. Dominique helps you compare those changes with your original priorities and limits.If There Are Multiple OffersFocus on the terms you are comfortable with rather than reacting emotionally to competition. The goal is still to make a decision that works for you.If the Offer Is DeclinedA declined offer does not erase the work you already did. Keep the search moving with a clearer sense of what you want and what you are willing to offer.Plan Your Home SearchBuy With DominiqueUnderstanding the Terms Behind an OfferAn offer includes more than a price. Financing, deposits, contingencies, included items, deadlines, and possession timing can affect the transaction. A term that appears simple in a conversation may have a different effect once it is written into the agreement, so review the contract before making a commitment.Compare the proposed terms with the property condition, lender requirements, and the level of uncertainty you can accept. Removing a protection does not remove the underlying issue it was intended to address. Keep track of the applicable review and response dates so a decision is based on understood obligations rather than pressure to move quickly.Understanding Written Loan TermsCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.Ask which conditions remain before approval and what changes require a new review. New debt, a change in employment or documented income, or a property issue can affect financing before closing. Use the lender’s current disclosures and explanations rather than relying on a general program description as a promise of eligibility or final terms.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan Estimates

first-time-pre-approval.html.main_text: Getting Preapproved for Your First HomeChoose a comfortable budget, gather your documents, and ask a lender to review your situation. The preapproval helps you focus your search while identifying issues to resolve before an offer.Build a search around your comfort levelThe amount a lender is willing to lend may be higher than the payment you want. Share your monthly target and cash budget with Dominique so the property search reflects your priorities.Keep the lender informedAsk what assumptions support the letter and what conditions remain. Report changes in employment, debt, or available funds to the lender before relying on the earlier review.01Set your comfort levelMonthly payment and cash available02Prepare documentsIncome, assets, and debts03Request a reviewAsk about options and conditions04Begin the searchUse a price range that fits your planCalifornia and San Fernando Valley contextFinancing a San Fernando Valley home should be evaluated with the actual purchase price and property costs, not just a headline loan amount. Dominique can help with the real estate side while a licensed lender explains qualification, rates, cash to close, and loan program rules.Understanding a Preliminary Lending DecisionA preapproval or prequalification letter can help establish a starting point for a search, but it does not complete the financing process. Ask what income, funds, debts, and credit information were reviewed, how current that review is, and which conditions remain. Lenders do not always use the two terms in exactly the same way.A selected property still needs to meet applicable appraisal, title, insurance, and program requirements. Keep the lender informed about changes to income, employment, debts, or available purchase funds. The useful purpose of an early review is to understand a realistic starting position and unresolved issues, rather than to treat the letter as unconditional final approval.Understanding Written Loan TermsCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.Ask which conditions remain before approval and what changes require a new review. New debt, a change in employment or documented income, or a property issue can affect financing before closing. Use the lender’s current disclosures and explanations rather than relying on a general program description as a promise of eligibility or final terms.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesYour Financing OptionsReview the financing resources and connect with a lender when you are ready.Connect With a Lender

first-time-touring.html.main_text: Touring Homes as a First Time BuyerTouring homes helps you compare the actual layout, condition, location, and everyday usefulness of properties within your budget. Keep your priorities consistent from one showing to the next, and distinguish what you can observe from what needs professional inspection.Before You TourReview your price range, location, must haves, and deal breakers before you arrive. That gives you something useful to compare at every showing.At the HomeLook at the layout, natural light, storage, condition, street, and neighborhood. Pay attention to the things that would be difficult or expensive to change.After the ShowingCompare the home with the others you have seen while the details are still fresh. Dominique helps you separate a strong fit from a home that simply photographed well.Plan Your Home SearchBuy With DominiqueDistinguishing Appearance From Property ConditionA well presented home can still have repair needs that are not visible during a showing. Review seller disclosures and arrange inspections appropriate to the property’s age, condition, and features. Questions about structure, drainage, electrical work, plumbing, or prior alterations may need a specialist rather than a general visual judgment.Evaluate the findings alongside your financing, insurance, and the deadlines in the purchase agreement. A repair estimate should describe the work being considered and any uncertainty that remains. Attractive finishes or a desirable location should not replace a clear understanding of material problems and the practical responsibility for addressing them.Understanding the Terms Behind an OfferAn offer includes more than a price. Financing, deposits, contingencies, included items, deadlines, and possession timing can affect the transaction. A term that appears simple in a conversation may have a different effect once it is written into the agreement, so review the contract before making a commitment.Compare the proposed terms with the property condition, lender requirements, and the level of uncertainty you can accept. Removing a protection does not remove the underlying issue it was intended to address. Keep track of the applicable review and response dates so a decision is based on understood obligations rather than pressure to move quickly.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan Estimates

homebuyer-financing-questions.html.main_text: FinancingExplore mortgage eligibility, down payments, credit, assistance, and the written loan terms that shape a home purchase.Pre Approval and Pre QualificationMortgage Preapproval and Prequalification ComparedBoth describe a lender’s preliminary willingness to lend under certain assumptions. Lenders use these terms differently, so ask what was actually checked and what conditions remain.Read MoreDown PaymentPlanning Your Down PaymentYour required down payment depends on the loan, the home, and your qualifications. Compare a few cash contributions, then include closing costs and the savings you want to keep after moving.Read MoreCredit ScoreCredit Scores and Mortgage QualificationThere is no single credit score that works for every mortgage. The loan program, lender, and the rest of your financial profile affect the decision. Ask a lender to review your actual situation.Read MoreAffordabilityFinding a Comfortable Home Purchase Price RangeStart with a monthly housing cost you can comfortably sustain and the cash you can use without exhausting your savings. A lender’s approval amount is only one part of that decision.Read More20% DownBuying a Home With Less Than Twenty Percent DownMany buyers can use a loan with less than 20% down if they qualify. The right comparison is the total cash required, monthly payment, insurance, and savings left after closing.Read MoreClosing CostsUnderstanding Homebuyer Closing CostsPlan for lender and settlement charges, applicable taxes, prepaid expenses, and any initial escrow deposit, in addition to your down payment. The Loan Estimate and Closing Disclosure show your transaction’s amounts.Read MoreStudent Loan DebtBuying a Home With Student Loan DebtYes, student debt does not automatically prevent a home purchase. The lender considers the payment required by the selected mortgage program along with your income and other debts.Read MorePre Approval DocumentsDocuments for Mortgage PreapprovalPrepare identification, income records, account statements, debt information, and evidence of your down payment funds. Your lender will give you a list based on your work, income, and loan program.Read More

Client Review★★★★★“I relocated to California and started my home search in the San Fernando Valley, looking at Chatsworth, Porter Ranch, and Granada Hills. Before we even toured a single home, Dominique sat down with me for a full buyer consultation and walked me through my finances, what I could actually afford, how the numbers worked, what to expect at every step. Coming from out of state, that alone took so much stress off the move. I ended up having to pause my search because of a job change, but she made such a strong impression that I already know exactly who I'm calling when I'm ready to start looking again!”Haley SimmonsClient Review★★★★★“First and foremost, Dominique is absolutely amazing!! She helped us find the perfect home and represented us completely and professionally throughout the entire process. She explained every step and answered all our questions completely. In the entire process, she went above and beyond, and exceeded all of our expectations. Before we selected our home, we asked her to take us to several others, and she arranged viewings and took us to each, reviewing the pros and cons with us. When we settled on this home, she explained every step and communicated to make sure everything was correct and on time. Dominique answered each of our questions and the purchase process and if there was something she wasn't sure of, she researched it in order to give us the best, and the correct, answer. I have made many home purchases in my lifetime, but this was the easiest I have ever experienced, due to Dominique. Dominique helped us determine what to offer, what sort of contingencies, escrow time, etc., to give us the best chance of acquiring this house. She was so thorough that our first offer was accepted! It made everything easy for us. I highly recommend Dominique! I will use her again if I sell or buy another property.”Nancy ParrisClient Review★★★★★“We recently had the pleasure of working with Dominique to purchase our first home, and we couldn’t be happier with the experience. From start to finish, their responsiveness, deep market knowledge, and strong negotiation skills made an incredibly stressful process feel manageable and even enjoyable. Their understanding of the local market was invaluable. Dominique helped us refine our search, educated us on neighborhood trends and pricing, and provided honest, data-driven insights on how to make a competitive yet sensible offer. We felt confident in every decision we made because we knew it was grounded in their expertise. Where Dominique truly shines is at the negotiation table. She advocated for us at every turn, helping us secure favorable terms and navigate some tricky back-and-forth with the sellers. Thanks to their persistence and strategic approach, we were able to close on a home we love, at a price and with conditions that worked for us. We’re incredibly grateful to Dominique for helping us close on our first home and would enthusiastically recommend them to anyone looking for a dedicated, knowledgeable, and highly effective real estate agent.”Corey FontenotClient Review★★★★★“Dominique takes great pride in providing quality service to her clients and it was evident in my experience with her when buying a house. She was patient and supportive during the search, which eventually led to finding the perfect home. She demonstrated expertise and creativity when it came to making a compelling offer that would be accepted by the seller in an extremely competitive market/neighborhood, while not compromising our budget. She was also attentive to details during the escrow process, which made me feel reassured. Her clear communication between all parties involved was excellent and appreciated. These are qualities that I do not overlook and I am certain contributed to the relative ease in the process of buying a house.”Goli AlamdarriClient Review★★★★★“Managing multiple rental homes from out of state was becoming overwhelming, and bringing in the right help made a huge difference. Communication was clear and consistent, which gave me real peace of mind. Dom handled both short-term and long-term rentals smoothly, from tenant coordination and turnovers to ongoing maintenance. Each property was managed with the right strategy, and everything ran efficiently.”Braxton SandersClient Review★★★★★“We worked together for several years managing multiple rental properties, and the experience was consistently smooth and well organized. The portfolio included a mix of short-term and mid-term leasing, and everything from tenant coordination to operational details was handled thoughtfully. What we appreciated most was the ability to adapt the rental strategy depending on what made the most sense for each property. Whether it was preparing a unit for new guests, managing turnovers, or keeping the financial side of things organized, the properties stayed occupied and performing well. It made owning and managing several rentals much easier than trying to do it ourselves.”Mark WilliamsClient Review★★★★★“I travel often and was having a hard time keeping up with my rental property, and I was honestly hesitant about using a property manager. That hesitation quickly went away — the entire experience was organized, responsive, and far easier than I expected. Tenant placement, maintenance, and service were handled smoothly, and I never felt out of the loop. The property stayed in great shape and consistently occupied, which gave me real peace of mind. I highly recommend Dominique’s property management services. She’s incredibly professional and always goes above and beyond.”Sandra WoodClient Review★★★★★“Dominique has done an excellent job managing my four-plex in Los Angeles, particularly with sourcing and screening high-quality tenants. I would confidently recommend her for any property management or real estate services.”Jeremy BroadousClient Review★★★★★“I had the pleasure of working with Dominique for over five years while she managed multiple rental properties for me. What truly sets her apart is her ability to anticipate potential issues before they become major problems. If anything significant ever came up, she handled it swiftly and with great care, always keeping my best interest at the forefront. I would highly recommend Dominique to anyone looking to work with a knowledgeable and dependable real estate professional in any capacity.”Nina Patel

03Finishes + FurnishingsMaterials, furniture, and the final details, selected together for the space.

Finish palettesWood tones, stone, tile, paint, lighting, and fabrics are edited so the space feels cohesive instead of busy.
Scale and layoutFurniture direction is planned around room size, traffic flow, comfort, and the way people actually live or work in the space.
Art and stylingArtwork, mirrors, greenery, textiles, and decor bring warmth and personality without making the room feel cluttered.

ListenDominique starts with how the space is used, what feels wrong now, and what the finished room needs to support.
EditLayout, scale, colors, finishes, and furniture direction are refined so the design does not feel random.
SourceMaterials, furniture, lighting, and styling pieces are chosen with quality, proportion, and budget in mind.
FinishThe final layer brings the space together so it feels warm, polished, and ready to live or work in.




05DesignFlooring, paint, tile, furniture sourcing, decor, artwork, and practical design choices before a project begins.Design


Design should make the space feel easier to love.Share your plans, priorities, and timing with Dominique.

jumbo-loans.html.main_text: Jumbo Loans and Conforming Loan LimitsA jumbo mortgage may be needed when the amount borrowed exceeds the applicable conforming limit for the county and property type. A high purchase price alone does not decide this, because the down payment affects the loan amount.Use the limit for the propertyConforming loan limits depend on the year, county, and number of units. Compare the amount borrowed with the current Federal Housing Finance Agency limit for the property rather than using the national baseline alone.Compare lender requirementsLoans above the applicable conforming limit may use jumbo financing. Down payment, reserves, credit, and pricing vary by lender. Ask for the exact qualification and reserve requirements before making an offer.County LimitReview the current limit for the county and property type.01Purchase priceThe agreed property price02Less down paymentYour contribution to the price03Loan amountCompare with the county limitCalifornia and San Fernando Valley contextFor a San Fernando Valley purchase, the lender determines eligibility and loan terms, while the property can add costs such as taxes, HOA dues, insurance, repairs, and appraisal related issues. Compare written lender disclosures with the full cost of the specific home.Understanding Written Loan TermsCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.Ask which conditions remain before approval and what changes require a new review. New debt, a change in employment or documented income, or a property issue can affect financing before closing. Use the lender’s current disclosures and explanations rather than relying on a general program description as a promise of eligibility or final terms.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesFederal Housing Finance Agency, Conforming Loan LimitsYour Financing OptionsReview the financing resources and connect with a lender when you are ready.Connect With a Lender

Connect with a Lender
Financing that fits your plans.Buying a home starts with a budget that works for you. A lending professional can explain your options, and Dominique can help you connect with one.
Your starting pointWhat feels comfortable for you?Your personalized home request should reflect your day-to-day life as well as the purchase price. Before meeting with a lender, think about the monthly cost, available savings, and timing you have in mind.01Your monthly budgetConsider your regular expenses and the housing payment you want to plan around.02Your available savingsThink about a down payment, closing costs, and funds you want to keep available after the move.03Your home plansShare your preferred area, the type of property, and when you would like to buy.
A closer look at the numbersYour down payment,shown simply.Adjust the example to see the part you would pay upfront and the remaining purchase amount.Example purchase price$Down payment percentage0%10%40%5%10%20%10%down paymentDown payment$60,000Remaining purchase amount$540,000Illustration only. Purchase price minus down payment, before any financed fees. Closing costs, interest, taxes, insurance, and other costs are not included. These example percentages are not loan offers or eligibility requirements.
Compare the detailsLook at the full loan offer.When you receive Loan Estimates, compare the same loan amount and type of loan. The rate is one part of the decision.Monthly costsReview the payment and any amounts for taxes, insurance, or mortgage insurance.Cash needed at closingLook at the down payment, closing costs, credits, and adjustments.Terms and timingReview the loan term, rate, fees, and the lender’s expected closing timeframe.Connect With a Lender

life-changes/death/can-i-keep-the-house-.main_text: Keeping a Home After Losing a Spouse’s IncomeKeeping the home after losing a spouse’s income may be possible if the ongoing expenses can be supported or an appropriate loan option is available. Contact the mortgage servicer and review ownership, benefits, income, and realistic housing alternatives before payments become difficult.Loan modification programsMany lenders offer loan modification options for surviving spouses facing hardship, which can adjust the interest rate, extend the loan term, or otherwise lower the monthly payment to a more sustainable level based on the surviving spouse's income alone.Life insurance and other assetsIf the deceased spouse had life insurance, those proceeds can sometimes be used to pay down the mortgage balance significantly, reducing the monthly payment enough to make it affordable, or to pay off the loan entirely in some cases.When downsizing becomes the practical choiceIf neither modification nor available assets make the current home affordable, selling and moving to a smaller, less expensive home, potentially using proceeds from the sale to buy outright or with a much smaller loan, is often a more sustainable long term path than continuing with a payment that does not fit the available budget.Survivor benefits that may help bridge the gapBeyond life insurance, Social Security survivor benefits, a pension's survivor option if the deceased spouse had one, or veterans' benefits if applicable can meaningfully supplement household income, and it's worth reviewing all potential benefit sources before assuming the mortgage is unaffordable on remaining income alone.California and San Fernando Valley contextWhen a San Fernando Valley home still has a mortgage after a death, the loan does not simply disappear. Confirm who has rights in the property, contact the servicer, and separate the mortgage question from the later real estate decision about keeping, selling, or renting the home.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/can-i-live-in-a-house.main_text: Living in a Home You InheritedYou may be able to live in an inherited home once ownership and estate issues are resolved, but mortgage, taxes, insurance and other heirs' rights still matter. Confirm the legal and financial details first.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.Compare keeping, renting, and selling with real numbersKeeping the home preserves the property but also preserves taxes, insurance, maintenance, and management responsibility. Renting may create income but adds landlord duties, vacancy risk, repairs, and legal requirements. Selling converts the property to cash but ends future ownership. The decision should use net proceeds and net rental income rather than gross estimates.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. Dominique can help assess value, repairs, cleanout, local buyer expectations, and sale timing without giving legal or tax advice.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. A house with no mortgage can still require insurance, property taxes, repairs, and ongoing attention. An inherited share may also mean decisions must be coordinated with other owners or an estate representative.Compare keeping, renting, or selling using the same information about the property. A home that is meaningful to the family may be practical to retain, but that decision should account for who will live there, manage it, and meet its expenses. Where authority or ownership is unsettled, obtain legal advice before signing agreements or making commitments on behalf of others.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/can-i-sell-a-house-th.main_text: Selling a House During ProbateA house may be sold during probate when the person acting for the estate has the required authority and follows the applicable procedure. The court documents and form of administration determine the notices, approvals, and timing involved.Court approval requirementsDepending on the type of probate, full probate versus a simplified process for smaller estates, selling the home may require formal court approval before or after accepting an offer, adding a legal step not present in typical home sales.The overbid processIn some probate sales, particularly under full court supervision, an accepted offer must go through a court confirmation hearing, where other interested buyers can appear and submit competing bids, sometimes resulting in the home ultimately selling for more than the originally accepted offer.Simplified probate alternativesEstates that qualify for a streamlined process, often called independent administration, may allow the executor to sell the property without court confirmation, significantly speeding up the sale process compared to a fully court supervised probate.Small estate proceduresMany states offer an expedited process for estates below a certain total value threshold, sometimes allowing property to transfer via a simplified affidavit process rather than formal probate at all, an option worth checking specifically if the estate's total value is relatively modest.California and San Fernando Valley contextIn California, the authority to transfer or sell a home after a death depends on title, estate documents, and whether a probate or another transfer procedure applies. A San Fernando Valley sale should not be marketed until the person with legal authority is identified.Understanding Estate Authority and the PropertyAn estate can involve several different decisions, including identifying beneficiaries, handling outstanding obligations, and establishing who may sign for a sale. Those decisions are related but not interchangeable. The person named to receive a house may still need an authorized representative to act while administration is underway. Review the estate documents and any court orders before treating the property as ready to transfer.The condition of the home and its ongoing expenses remain relevant while authority is being resolved. Insurance, utilities, security, and necessary maintenance may need attention before a buyer is involved. Keep a record of work and payments, and ask the estate’s legal adviser who can authorize them. A real estate timeline should reflect the actual administration requirements rather than a promised closing date.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/can-siblings-force-th.main_text: Resolving Disagreements About Selling an Inherited HomeAn inherited home may eventually be sold through a legal process when its owners cannot agree, but no sibling should assume they can act for everyone. Ownership, estate administration, and applicable coownership law determine the available options.The partition action processAny co owner generally has the legal right to file a partition action, asking a court to order the property sold and proceeds divided, even if other co owners object, since courts generally don't force unwilling co owners to remain jointly tied to a property indefinitely.Alternatives to a court ordered saleBefore resorting to a partition action, siblings can negotiate a buyout, where one sibling purchases the others' shares, or agree to a structured timeline for eventually selling, both of which avoid the cost and family strain of formal litigation.Costs and downsides of a partition actionPartition actions typically take 6 months to over a year and can cost tens of thousands of dollars in legal fees, split among the co owners from the eventual sale proceeds, making it a genuinely costly last resort rather than a first option.Mediation as a step before litigationMany family law and probate attorneys recommend mediation with a neutral third party before filing a partition action, since a mediated agreement is typically faster and considerably less expensive than full litigation, and it can preserve family relationships that a contested court battle often damages further.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. Dominique can help assess value, repairs, cleanout, local buyer expectations, and sale timing without giving legal or tax advice.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. A house with no mortgage can still require insurance, property taxes, repairs, and ongoing attention. An inherited share may also mean decisions must be coordinated with other owners or an estate representative.Compare keeping, renting, or selling using the same information about the property. A home that is meaningful to the family may be practical to retain, but that decision should account for who will live there, manage it, and meet its expenses. Where authority or ownership is unsettled, obtain legal advice before signing agreements or making commitments on behalf of others.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/do-i-have-to-pay-off-.main_text: Understanding a Parent’s Mortgage After Their DeathYou do not automatically become personally responsible for your parent’s mortgage just because you inherit the home. Inheriting a home doesn't mean personally taking on the deceased's mortgage debt as a new financial obligation.How mortgage debt is actually handledThe mortgage remains attached to the property itself, not the heir personally. If the estate has enough assets or life insurance proceeds to pay it off, that's often the simplest path. Otherwise, an heir keeping the home typically needs to continue making payments or refinance the loan into their own name.Federal protections for heirsFederal law, specifically the Garn St. Germain Act generally allows an heir to assume an existing mortgage's terms, including the interest rate, without the loan being called due immediately, which can be valuable if the original rate was lower than current market rates.What happens if no one wants to keep making paymentsIf no heir wants to take over payments or the home can't otherwise be paid off, the property is typically sold, either voluntarily by the heirs or, if payments lapse long enough, potentially through foreclosure, though heirs generally have a reasonable window to sell before this becomes a serious risk.Contacting the servicer proactivelyNotifying the mortgage servicer of the owner's death as soon as possible, even before deciding what to do with the home, helps ensure heirs receive proper notices and avoid an unnecessary default or foreclosure process starting simply because the servicer wasn't aware of the situation and payments lapsed without anyone realizing.California and San Fernando Valley contextWhen a San Fernando Valley home still has a mortgage after a death, the loan does not simply disappear. Confirm who has rights in the property, contact the servicer, and separate the mortgage question from the later real estate decision about keeping, selling, or renting the home.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. A house with no mortgage can still require insurance, property taxes, repairs, and ongoing attention. An inherited share may also mean decisions must be coordinated with other owners or an estate representative.Compare keeping, renting, or selling using the same information about the property. A home that is meaningful to the family may be practical to retain, but that decision should account for who will live there, manage it, and meet its expenses. Where authority or ownership is unsettled, obtain legal advice before signing agreements or making commitments on behalf of others.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/do-i-have-to-refinanc.main_text: Mortgage Options After a Spouse DiesRefinancing is not automatically required after a spouse dies. Refinancing isn't an automatic requirement, and many surviving spouses can continue with the existing mortgage under federal succession protections.Why refinancing often isn't necessaryAs a recognized successor in interest, a surviving spouse can typically continue making payments on the existing mortgage under its original terms, meaning no new loan application, credit check, or qualification process is required simply to maintain the status quo.When refinancing makes sense anywayRefinancing can still be worthwhile if the original interest rate is significantly higher than current rates, if the surviving spouse wants to remove any ambiguity by formally putting the loan in their own name, or if they want to change the loan term or tap into home equity for other financial needs.The formal title transfer processSeparate from the mortgage itself, transferring the property's title fully into the surviving spouse's name, if it wasn't already held jointly, generally involves recording an affidavit of death along with the property's existing deed, a simpler process than a full refinance.Updating homeowners insurance after the transferOnce title is transferred, updating the homeowners insurance policy to reflect the surviving spouse as the sole named insured is an important, easily overlooked step, since a policy still listing a deceased person alone can create complications if a claim needs to be filed later.California and San Fernando Valley contextWhen a San Fernando Valley home still has a mortgage after a death, the loan does not simply disappear. Confirm who has rights in the property, contact the servicer, and separate the mortgage question from the later real estate decision about keeping, selling, or renting the home.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. life-changes/death/do-i-owe-taxes-on-a-h.main_text: Understanding Taxes on an Inherited HouseInheriting a house can involve property tax reassessment and tax consequences when the property is later sold or rented. Federal income tax basis rules and California Proposition 19 are separate issues, so review both before assuming that the transfer leaves your taxes unchanged.Federal Income Tax BasisInherited property generally receives a basis determined under federal rules, often with reference to the value at the owner’s death. Exceptions, alternative valuation rules, and later adjustments may matter. Retain valuation and improvement records so a tax professional can evaluate a later sale using the appropriate adjusted basis.California Property Tax ReassessmentCalifornia property tax treatment is separate from federal income tax basis. Proposition 19 can affect an inherited family home, with eligibility tied to the transfer, relationship, use, value, and filings. Do not assume that an heir’s future tax bill will match the previous owner’s bill.The Property’s Later UseSelling, renting, or occupying the inherited home can lead to different tax considerations. Review the estate records and planned use before treating a tax exclusion or prior valuation as applicable. An attorney can address estate authority, while a tax professional and county assessor can address their respective tax issues.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor inherited property in California, federal basis rules and California property tax reassessment rules can affect the numbers, while title and estate documents determine who can act. Use the current IRS and California Board of Equalization guidance and consult a qualified tax professional for the specific estate.Distinguishing the Taxes That May ApplyThe value used for federal income tax calculations is different from the taxable value used for California property taxes. An inherited home can have one basis for a later sale and a separate reassessment outcome for annual property taxes. Keep documentation of the transfer date, property value, improvements, and subsequent use so a tax professional can evaluate the relevant rules.California Proposition 19 does not preserve every inherited property’s prior taxable value. Eligibility can depend on the relationship between the parties, use of the home, value, and required filings. Review the current Board of Equalization guidance and confirm the property’s circumstances with the county assessor. An exclusion should be verified before using a prior owner’s tax bill as your future budget.SourcesInternal Revenue Service, Basis of AssetsCalifornia Board of Equalization, Proposition 19California Courts, Property After a DeathSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/do-we-have-to-go-thro.main_text: Determining Whether Probate Is Needed Before a Home SaleProbate depends on how title was held and what estate documents exist. Confirm who has legal authority before signing a listing or sale agreement.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.A mortgage usually remains attached to the propertyA death does not automatically erase the loan. Payments, insurance, taxes, and maintenance may continue while ownership or estate authority is resolved. Contact the servicer, preserve payment records, and ask what documentation is required. Do not assume that taking title automatically makes an heir personally liable for the deceased borrower’s debt.California and San Fernando Valley contextIn California, the authority to transfer or sell a home after a death depends on title, estate documents, and whether a probate or another transfer procedure applies. A San Fernando Valley sale should not be marketed until the person with legal authority is identified.Understanding Estate Authority and the PropertyAn estate can involve several different decisions, including identifying beneficiaries, handling outstanding obligations, and establishing who may sign for a sale. Those decisions are related but not interchangeable. The person named to receive a house may still need an authorized representative to act while administration is underway. Review the estate documents and any court orders before treating the property as ready to transfer.The condition of the home and its ongoing expenses remain relevant while authority is being resolved. Insurance, utilities, security, and necessary maintenance may need attention before a buyer is involved. Keep a record of work and payments, and ask the estate’s legal adviser who can authorize them. A real estate timeline should reflect the actual administration requirements rather than a promised closing date.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/how-do-i-clean-out-an.main_text: Clearing Belongings and Preparing an Inherited Home for SaleStart by securing important documents and valuables, then sort the belongings before clearing the home or preparing it for sale. Clearing decades of accumulated belongings is often one of the more emotionally and logistically demanding parts of handling an inherited property.Sorting into categoriesMost families find it helpful to sort belongings into clear categories early: items to keep as keepsakes, items to sell, items to donate, and items to discard, rather than trying to make every decision item by item as they go.Estate sale and liquidation servicesBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. A house with no mortgage can still require insurance, property taxes, repairs, and ongoing attention. An inherited share may also mean decisions must be coordinated with other owners or an estate representative.Junk removal and donation optionsWatching for items with overlooked valueBefore committing everything to donation or disposal, having a professional briefly assess items like jewelry, coins, art, or collectibles can prevent accidentally discarding or underselling something with meaningful value that isn't obvious to a family member without specific expertise in appraising such items.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. Dominique can help assess value, repairs, cleanout, local buyer expectations, and sale timing without giving legal or tax advice.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeCompare keeping, renting, or selling using the same information about the property. A home that is meaningful to the family may be practical to retain, but that decision should account for who will live there, manage it, and meet its expenses. Where authority or ownership is unsettled, obtain legal advice before signing agreements or making commitments on behalf of others.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/how-long-does-it-take.main_text: Understanding the Timeline for Selling an Inherited HouseThe timeline depends on the market, financing or legal steps, and how quickly the parties can move forward. life-changes/death/i-inherited-a-house-b.main_text: Managing an Inherited House From a DistanceYou can manage an inherited property from another area, but you may need local help for access, repairs, cleanout, maintenance and the sale. Start by securing the home and confirming who has authority to make decisions.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.An inherited home can be handled from a distanceSecure the property, confirm insurance coverage, arrange mail and utilities, document condition and belongings, and identify a reliable local contact. Remote signatures and vendor coordination are possible, but someone may still need to provide access for inspections, repairs, appraisal, and personal property removal.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. Dominique can help assess value, repairs, cleanout, local buyer expectations, and sale timing without giving legal or tax advice.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. A house with no mortgage can still require insurance, property taxes, repairs, and ongoing attention. An inherited share may also mean decisions must be coordinated with other owners or an estate representative.Compare keeping, renting, or selling using the same information about the property. A home that is meaningful to the family may be practical to retain, but that decision should account for who will live there, manage it, and meet its expenses. Where authority or ownership is unsettled, obtain legal advice before signing agreements or making commitments on behalf of others.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/i-inherited-a-house-t.main_text: Repairing an Inherited House or Selling in Its Current ConditionWhether to repair or sell as is depends on the home's condition, available cash, timeline and likely return from the improvements. Get realistic estimates before putting estate money into renovations.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.Compare repair cost with likely market impactObtain estimates for health, safety, structural, system, and cosmetic work. Then compare an as is price range with the likely price after repairs, the time required, carrying costs, available cash, and the risk of discovering additional problems. The project with the highest projected sale price does not always produce the highest net proceeds.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. Dominique can help assess value, repairs, cleanout, local buyer expectations, and sale timing without giving legal or tax advice.Evaluating Work Before CommittingSeparate necessary repairs from optional changes so the decision reflects the home’s actual condition. A cosmetic refresh, a failing system, and a structural problem have different implications for disruption, permits, financing, and the order of work. Written estimates should make the scope and exclusions clear rather than treating all improvements as one number.For California work that requires a licensed contractor, verify the relevant license and discuss permits with the local building authority. Existing alterations may also need review. Leave space for uncertainty before assuming a project can be completed within a particular move or sale timeline, and do not treat any improvement as a guaranteed increase in resale value.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesCalifornia Contractors State License Board, Hiring a ContractorSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/is-my-name-automatica.main_text: Understanding Home Title After a Spouse DiesMarriage alone does not automatically add your name to a deceased spouse’s home title. An attorney can determine the appropriate California transfer process from the actual deed and estate documents.Checking for a transfer on death deedSome states allow a transfer on death deed to be recorded during the original owner's lifetime, which functions similarly to a beneficiary designation and avoids probate even without joint tenancy, worth checking for specifically since it isn't as commonly used or discussed as a trust or joint tenancy.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. life-changes/death/my-dad-died-and-his-n.main_text: Selling a Home Still Titled in a Deceased Parent’s NameYes, but the person with legal authority over the property or estate must be identified before the sale can move forward. The right to sell depends on title, estate documents and whether probate or another legal process is required. Do not sign a listing or sale agreement until the person with legal authority over the property has been identified.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.A mortgage usually remains attached to the propertyA death does not automatically erase the loan. Payments, insurance, taxes, and maintenance may continue while ownership or estate authority is resolved. Contact the servicer, preserve payment records, and ask what documentation is required. Do not assume that taking title automatically makes an heir personally liable for the deceased borrower’s debt.California and San Fernando Valley contextIn California, the authority to transfer or sell a home after a death depends on title, estate documents, and whether a probate or another transfer procedure applies. A San Fernando Valley sale should not be marketed until the person with legal authority is identified.Separating Ownership From Mortgage ObligationsA deed describes ownership, while a mortgage or deed of trust relates to the loan secured by the home. Changing one does not necessarily change the other. Before a transfer, review the recorded ownership documents, outstanding loans, and the authority of each person involved. A name appearing in one document is not a substitute for understanding the complete arrangement.Keep copies of the documents that explain the proposed change and its timing. A title company can identify recorded matters, an attorney can explain legal rights, and the lender or servicer can address loan requirements. Coordinate those explanations before signing away an interest, accepting a new obligation, or assuming that a transfer resolves all remaining responsibilities.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/my-husband-died-what-.main_text: Understanding Your Home After Your Husband DiesBefore deciding whether to keep or sell, confirm who owns the property now, whether there is a mortgage, and whether an estate or probate process applies. Once authority is clear, you can evaluate value, costs, condition and your own needs.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.A mortgage usually remains attached to the propertyA death does not automatically erase the loan. Payments, insurance, taxes, and maintenance may continue while ownership or estate authority is resolved. Contact the servicer, preserve payment records, and ask what documentation is required. Do not assume that taking title automatically makes an heir personally liable for the deceased borrower’s debt.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. Dominique can help assess value, repairs, cleanout, local buyer expectations, and sale timing without giving legal or tax advice.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. A house with no mortgage can still require insurance, property taxes, repairs, and ongoing attention. An inherited share may also mean decisions must be coordinated with other owners or an estate representative.Compare keeping, renting, or selling using the same information about the property. A home that is meaningful to the family may be practical to retain, but that decision should account for who will live there, manage it, and meet its expenses. life-changes/death/my-sibling-wants-to-k.main_text: Keeping or Selling an Inherited Home When Siblings DisagreeWhen siblings disagree about an inherited home, possible resolutions include an agreed sale, one owner buying another’s share, or appropriate legal proceedings. Confirm ownership and estate authority first, because one beneficiary’s preference does not establish the right to act for everyone.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.Co owners need a documented planIdentify each ownership interest, the expenses paid by each person, whether anyone occupies the home, and whether one owner can realistically buy out the others. If everyone agrees to sell, decide who will handle access, repairs, belongings, and communication. If owners cannot agree, legal advice may be necessary before the property can move forward.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor an inherited or family home in the San Fernando Valley, the real estate decision often comes after title, estate authority, condition, carrying costs, and family goals are clarified. Dominique can help assess value, repairs, cleanout, local buyer expectations, and sale timing without giving legal or tax advice.Evaluating the Inherited Property as a WholeBefore choosing a use for an inherited home, establish its condition, recorded ownership, outstanding obligations, and the rights of everyone involved. A house with no mortgage can still require insurance, property taxes, repairs, and ongoing attention. An inherited share may also mean decisions must be coordinated with other owners or an estate representative.Compare keeping, renting, or selling using the same information about the property. A home that is meaningful to the family may be practical to retain, but that decision should account for who will live there, manage it, and meet its expenses. Where authority or ownership is unsettled, obtain legal advice before signing agreements or making commitments on behalf of others.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique

life-changes/death/my-spouse-died-and-i-.main_text: Housing Options When a Surviving Spouse Cannot Afford the HomeIf a spouse has died and the home is no longer affordable, review the mortgage, insurance, taxes, income and available equity before making a rushed decision. Selling or moving may be options, but first confirm title and estate requirements.Confirm who has authority before making property decisionsThe deed, trust, will, court documents, and mortgage records may all affect what can happen next. Being named in a will does not always mean a person can immediately sign a listing agreement or deed. Before accepting an offer, transferring ownership, or spending heavily on repairs, confirm who currently holds title and who has legal authority to act for the property or estate.A mortgage usually remains attached to the propertyA death does not automatically erase the loan. Payments, insurance, taxes, and maintenance may continue while ownership or estate authority is resolved. Contact the servicer, preserve payment records, and ask what documentation is required. Do not assume that taking title automatically makes an heir personally liable for the deceased borrower’s debt.California and San Fernando Valley contextWhen a San Fernando Valley home still has a mortgage after a death, the loan does not simply disappear. Confirm who has rights in the property, contact the servicer, and separate the mortgage question from the later real estate decision about keeping, selling, or renting the home.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesCalifornia Courts, Property After a DeathConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Inherited Home MortgagesSelling With DominiqueSee how Dominique can help with the real estate side of your property.Sell With Dominique
