life-changes/growing-family/what-neighbo.main_text: Evaluating Neighborhood Safety Before Buying a HomeLook at the specific street, the routes your household would use, and current information from the local public agencies. For a family with young children, traffic, crossings, sidewalks, visibility, and the property itself deserve attention alongside reported crime.Visit the street at different timesObserve weekday traffic, evening lighting, parking, visibility at driveways, and the walk to nearby destinations. If your children would walk or cycle, look at the actual route and crossings rather than judging from distance alone.Read reported crime information in contextUse the police agency serving the address. For LAPD areas, review its Crime Mapping and COMPSTAT resources. Check the reporting period and geographic coverage; a snapshot is not a guarantee about future safety. Ask the agency about gaps or unfamiliar categories.Inspect the property’s practical risksLook at gates, fences, stairs, pool access, visibility from the street, and the condition of doors and windows. Have the appropriate inspectors assess property conditions before your purchase deadlines. A quiet street does not replace a careful inspection.Ask specific questions and make your own comparisonAsk about traffic at school pickup, the nearest crossing, street lighting, and issues residents have actually observed. Compare the same factors for each property you are considering. No neighborhood can be promised to be risk free.Testing Location Against Everyday LifeA neighborhood comparison becomes clearer when it is tied to the trips and services you actually use. Check travel times for your usual schedule, parking arrangements, nearby errands, public transportation where relevant, and the setting of the specific street. Conditions can change within a community, so a familiar neighborhood name is only a starting point.Visit when practical and verify facts through the appropriate public sources. School assignments should be checked with the district for the address, and planned development or zoning should be checked with the governing jurisdiction. Avoid relying on broad claims about who lives in an area or guarantees about future demand when assessing whether a location fits your household.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/growing-family/whats-the-be.main_text: Verifying School Assignments for a San Fernando Valley HomeStart with the exact property address, your child’s grade, and the school year you expect to enroll. Check the district’s official school lookup, then confirm the result with its enrollment office before relying on a school assignment when buying a home in the San Fernando Valley.Find the school assigned to the addressFirst identify the district that serves the property. For an address within LAUSD, use its Resident School Identifier. A nearby school, a neighborhood name, or a school listed in a real estate advertisement is not enough to confirm where your child can enroll.Confirm the details with the districtGive the enrollment office the full address and ask which school serves the relevant grade and school year. Ask what documents are needed, whether a boundary change affects the address, and whether anything else must be confirmed. Save the response with your home search notes.Check whether the program has a separate applicationA neighborhood school assignment and admission to a magnet, charter, transfer, or other choice program can involve different processes. Ask the program directly about applications, deadlines, eligibility, and available places. Buying a nearby home should not be treated as a promise of admission.Decide whether the school works for your childOnce you know the enrollment options, ask about learning support, language programs, class schedules, after school care, and transportation. Review the California School Dashboard alongside information from school staff, and visit when available. These details help you judge the fit for your child without reducing the decision to one rating.Check the school day alongside the homeTry the trip between the property, school, childcare, and work at the times you would actually travel. Compare that routine with the home’s price, layout, and monthly costs. Dominique can help with the property search; the district confirms school enrollment.Testing Location Against Everyday LifeA neighborhood comparison becomes clearer when it is tied to the trips and services you actually use. Check travel times for your usual schedule, parking arrangements, nearby errands, public transportation where relevant, and the setting of the specific street. Conditions can change within a community, so a familiar neighborhood name is only a starting point.Visit when practical and verify facts through the appropriate public sources. School assignments should be checked with the district for the address, and planned development or zoning should be checked with the governing jurisdiction. Avoid relying on broad claims about who lives in an area or guarantees about future demand when assessing whether a location fits your household.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

Review whether rearranging the existing space can solve those problems before assuming a larger purchase is necessary.Read MoreAdd On Or MoveComparing a Home Addition With Moving to a Larger HouseA home addition and a move can have very different expenses, and neither is always the less expensive choice. Compare a feasible, permitted addition with actual replacement properties, including disruption, financing, transaction expenses, and the ongoing budget afterward.Read MoreBedroom NeedsPlanning Bedroom Space for Two ChildrenThe number of bedrooms that works for your household depends on privacy, routines, room layout, budget, and how you want to use the space.Read MoreMoving TimelineConsidering a Move Before and After a Baby Is BornMoving before a baby arrives can allow time to settle in, while moving afterward may provide more certainty about the household’s routines and needs. Consider health, support, housing readiness, and the flexibility of the timeline rather than relying on a universal best date.Read MoreSchool DecisionsVerifying School Assignments for a San Fernando Valley HomeStart with the exact property address, your child’s grade, and the school year you expect to enroll. Check the district’s official school lookup, then confirm the result with its enrollment office before relying on a school assignment when buying a home in the San Fernando Valley.Read MoreAffordabilityEvaluating a Larger Home on One Income With a New BabyA larger home may be affordable on one income if the complete housing payment and other household expenses fit the income you expect after the baby arrives. Review financing and your own budget using that changed income, rather than the earnings you receive today.Read MoreFamily Outdoor SpaceEvaluating a Yard for a Home With Young ChildrenA yard is one of the more debated features for families with young children, valuable for many, but not universally necessary depending on the neighborhood and family's lifestyle.Read MoreCost & SavingsUnderstanding a Garage Conversion for a Nursery or PlayroomA garage conversion’s expenses depend on whether the proposed nursery or playroom is feasible, permitted, and suitable for the property. life-changes/marriage/buy-a-house-before.main_text: Comparing a Home Purchase Before and After the WeddingPut both goals on one cash flow plan. Compare the wedding budget, cash needed to buy, emergency savings, and the monthly payment you can handle after the wedding so one goal does not weaken the other.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.Compare buying now with waitingBuying sooner may lock in a home that fits the next stage, while waiting can preserve flexibility and give the household more time to build savings or understand its long term needs. Compare the cost of renting with the total cost of owning, including closing costs, maintenance, insurance, taxes, and the possibility of selling sooner than expected.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. life-changes/marriage/buying-a-home-toge.main_text: Buying Together When One Spouse Already Has a MortgageA prior mortgage can affect the debt used for qualification and the cash available for the next purchase. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.Ownership and the mortgage are not the sameThe deed identifies ownership, while the promissory note identifies who is responsible for repaying the loan. Adding a spouse to a deed does not add that spouse to the mortgage, and removing a name from title does not release a borrower from the debt. Review the recorded deed and loan documents before planning a sale, refinance, or ownership change.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/buying-a-house-tog.main_text: Buying Together With Different Credit Scores or DebtsYou may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.How joint mortgage qualification worksA couple does not always have to use both incomes or apply jointly. Including another borrower may add income, but it can also add that person’s debts and credit profile. Ask a lender to compare more than one application structure and show the rate, payment, cash required, and qualification result for each. Do not choose a structure based only on the largest approval amount.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding Credit in a Mortgage ReviewA mortgage review considers more than a single score. The lender evaluates credit history, current obligations, documented income, available funds, and the requirements of the chosen program. A score shown by a consumer service may also differ from the score or assessment used in a lending decision.Review your credit information for errors and discuss unresolved questions with the lender before changing accounts or borrowing again. Paying down a balance, closing an account, or taking on new debt can affect an application in different ways. An individual review is more useful than a universal score target presented as a guarantee of approval.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/can-married-couple.main_text: Using Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home PurchaseMarried couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The lender also reviews debts, credit, assets, and the property, so two incomes do not automatically mean approval.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.How joint mortgage qualification worksA couple does not always have to use both incomes or apply jointly. Including another borrower may add income, but it can also add that person’s debts and credit profile. Ask a lender to compare more than one application structure and show the rate, payment, cash required, and qualification result for each. Do not choose a structure based only on the largest approval amount.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/can-two-people-buy.main_text: Joint Home Buying When Only One Partner Has Strong CreditTwo people may be able to buy together with different credit profiles, but the financing options depend on how the lender evaluates each borrower. A joint application and an application by one borrower can produce different results and different ownership considerations.How lenders evaluate joint applicationsWhen two people apply for a mortgage together, most lenders base the loan's terms, particularly the interest rate, on the lower of the two credit scores, specifically the lower middle score, meaning each applicant's three credit bureau scores, Equifax, Experian, TransUnion are ranked and the middle score of each person is compared, with the lower of the two used for pricing. This means a gap of 100 points or more in credit can result in a noticeably higher interest rate than if the stronger credit partner applied alone, sometimes half a percentage point or more depending on the loan program.Applying with only one partner's name on the loanAn alternative is to have only the partner with stronger credit apply for and qualify for the mortgage individually, using their income and credit alone. Both partners can still be added to the property's title as co owners even if only one is on the note , the loan itself, separating who's legally responsible for the debt from who legally owns the property via the deed.The trade off of applying with just one partnerA mortgage review considers more than a single score. The lender evaluates credit history, current obligations, documented income, available funds, and the requirements of the chosen program. A score shown by a consumer service may also differ from the score or assessment used in a lending decision.Improving credit before applying togetherIf time allows, working to improve the lower credit score before applying, paying down balances, addressing any errors on the credit report, can sometimes close the gap enough to make a joint application with both names the more financially favorable option, since it would allow both incomes to be counted while securing a more competitive rate.How much time credit repair typically takesMeaningful credit score improvement, closing a gap of 50 100 points, often takes 3 6 months of consistent on time payments and reduced credit utilization, though disputing a specific reporting error can sometimes produce a faster jump if the dispute is resolved in the applicant's favor. Couples with more time before they need to buy have more room to close this gap than those hoping to purchase within the next month or two.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/do-we-need-to-be-m.main_text: Joint Mortgage Qualification for Unmarried BuyersYou do not have to be married to apply for a joint mortgage. Each applicant still needs to meet the lender’s requirements, and a separate ownership agreement can clarify contributions and responsibilities between unmarried buyers.What lenders actually evaluateMortgage lenders assess combined income, debt, credit history, and assets for any joint applicants, whether they're married, engaged, or simply purchasing a property together as unmarried partners, family members, or friends, requiring the same W 2s, pay stubs, and tax returns from each applicant regardless of relationship status. The underwriting process itself doesn't differentiate based on the relationship between applicants.What does change without marriageBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.How title and mortgage responsibility can differIt's possible for two unmarried people to both be on the mortgage, sharing equal responsibility for the debt via a promissory note and deed of trust, while structuring the property title differently, as joint tenants or tenants in common with specific ownership percentages recorded on the grant deed. These are two separate legal documents serving different purposes, and it's worth understanding both rather than assuming being on the loan automatically defines ownership shares.What unmarried co borrowers should plan forUnmarried couples applying for a joint mortgage benefit from the same upfront planning recommended for any co ownership situation, a clear written agreement about ownership shares, responsibility for payments, and what happens if one partner wants to sell or the relationship ends, since none of these questions are automatically answered by marital status the way they might be for a married couple.Estate planning considerations for unmarried co ownersA partner’s inheritance rights depend on the ownership arrangement, valid estate documents, and applicable law. Review title and estate planning together rather than assuming that a mortgage application or relationship status settles who will receive a share after a death.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/do-we-need-to-comb.main_text: Managing Shared Finances Before Buying a Home TogetherYou do not need to merge every account before buying a home together. You do need a clear understanding of purchase contributions, ongoing payments, savings, and the lender’s documentation requirements.What a lender actually needs to seeBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.How separate finances affect the mortgage applicationLenders will ask both applicants for full financial documentation, pay stubs, W 2s, two years of tax returns, and two to three months of bank statements, regardless of whether the couple shares accounts. What matters is that each person's individual financial picture is clear and verifiable, not that the money is pooled together in one place.Considerations beyond the mortgage itselfCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.What to decide before applyingRegardless of how finances are structured day to day, couples should have a clear agreement about who's responsible for what portion of the mortgage payment and other home related costs before applying, since ambiguity here tends to create friction once the obligation becomes real each month.What happens if one partner's contribution changesIncome changes, a job loss, a career shift, a new child, are common over the life of a mortgage, and couples who agree on a fixed percentage split early may need to revisit that arrangement later. Building in a plan for how contribution splits would be renegotiated, rather than assuming today's arrangement is permanent, avoids conflict if circumstances shift.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/getting-married-an.main_text: Choosing a Home When Combining HouseholdsStart with the people who will live there and the routines the home must support: bedrooms, privacy, work or school needs, storage, transportation, outdoor space, and the monthly cost. A larger home is useful only if it solves the household’s real day to day needs.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.How joint mortgage qualification worksA couple does not always have to use both incomes or apply jointly. Including another borrower may add income, but it can also add that person’s debts and credit profile. Ask a lender to compare more than one application structure and show the rate, payment, cash required, and qualification result for each. Do not choose a structure based only on the largest approval amount.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/how-do-newlyweds-a.main_text: Home Buying for Newlyweds With Student Loan DebtNewlyweds can still buy a home with student loan debt by choosing a payment and price range that work after the lender counts the required debt payments. Combining two incomes as a newly married couple can help offset the impact of student loan debt on affordability, but it requires understanding exactly how that debt factors into mortgage qualification.How lenders factor in combined student debtA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Loan programs that offer more flexibilityCompare financing using the written terms for your application and property. The loan amount, repayment period, rate structure, mortgage insurance, lender charges, and cash required at closing work together. A change in one part of the offer can affect the others, so a quoted monthly principal and interest payment is only part of the comparison.Strategies newlyweds commonly useCombining two incomes changes the picture significantlyEven with meaningful student debt, two full incomes applied jointly often provide substantially more borrowing power than either partner would have alone, which is one of the practical financial advantages of buying as a married couple rather than as a single applicant carrying the same debt.Refinancing or forgiveness programs that can help laterSome newlyweds qualify for a smaller loan now with the expectation that student loan refinancing, employer repayment assistance, or income driven forgiveness programs will reduce their debt burden over the following years, freeing up more of their income for other goals down the road, though it's worth treating any future forgiveness as a bonus rather than counting on it when calculating what to buy today.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/is-it-better-to-bu.main_text: Comparing Buying and Renting While Settling Into Married LifeBuying together may suit a couple with a lasting location plan, suitable financing, and a clear agreement about the home’s responsibilities. Continuing to rent can provide flexibility while work, finances, or shared priorities are still changing.Financial readiness signalsSigns that buying may make sense include having a stable combined income, an emergency fund covering three to six months of expenses kept separate from the down payment, manageable existing debt, and a down payment saved without depleting all other savings. Renting may remain the better choice if either partner's income or job situation is still unstable, or if a down payment would require using funds needed for other financial priorities.Relationship considerations beyond financesBuying a home together is a significant, often difficult to reverse financial commitment between two people. Couples who haven't yet combined finances in any way, or who are uncertain about the long term direction of the relationship, may find that renting together first offers a lower stakes way to test shared financial decision making before taking on a mortgage together.Local market conditions matter tooIn markets where rent costs are comparable to or higher than a mortgage payment for a similar property, buying can make financial sense even for a couple who might otherwise wait. In markets with relatively low rents compared to purchase prices, waiting and continuing to save may allow for a stronger down payment and better loan terms later.There's no fixed timeline that applies to everyoneSome couples buy together within their first year of dating, others wait until years into a marriage. The right timing depends entirely on the specific couple's finances, communication, and comfort level, not any external expectation about how "settled" a relationship needs to look before making this decision.The cost of waiting too long in a rising marketIn markets where home prices are appreciating faster than a couple's combined savings rate, waiting to feel more "ready" can mean the eventual purchase costs meaningfully more than it would have earlier, an important factor to weigh against the benefits of waiting for more financial cushion or relationship certainty.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/on-title-but-not-m.main_text:
Understanding Home Title Without Being on the MortgageBeing named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Not being named on the mortgage loan generally means you are not one of the borrowers personally responsible for making the loan payments, although the lender’s lien can still affect the property.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.Ownership and the mortgage are not the sameThe deed identifies ownership, while the promissory note identifies who is responsible for repaying the loan. Adding a spouse to a deed does not add that spouse to the mortgage, and removing a name from title does not release a borrower from the debt. Review the recorded deed and loan documents before planning a sale, refinance, or ownership change.The title and the mortgage do two different jobs. The deed is the recorded document used to show who holds ownership in the property.
The promissory note identifies who promised to repay the borrowed money. The deed of trust secures that debt against the property and gives the lender the right to pursue foreclosure if the loan is not paid as agreed.
Because these documents serve different purposes, a person can be an owner without being a borrower. That can happen when one spouse bought the home before marriage and later added the other spouse to the deed, or when a lender approved the loan using only one spouse's income and credit.
What being on the title usually means Your name should appear on the recorded deed, along with the way ownership is held. Being on title may give you an ownership interest and may require your signature before the property can be sold or transferred.
The exact rights attached to that interest depend on the wording of the deed, how title is held, and applicable California property law. What not being on the mortgage usually means If you did not sign the promissory note, you are generally not personally obligated to repay that loan.
The monthly payment may not appear as your individual debt in the same way it appears for the borrower. However, the loan is still secured by the home.
If the borrower stops paying, the property may still be subject to foreclosure even though another owner did not sign the note. Selling the home When the home is sold, the outstanding mortgage is normally paid from the closing proceeds before the owners receive the remaining equity.
Everyone whose ownership interest must be transferred will generally need to sign the required sale documents. Being off the loan does not automatically remove a person who is on title from the sale process.
Refinancing or changing the loan Adding someone to title does not add that person to the existing loan. Changing the borrowers usually requires a refinance, an approved loan assumption, or another process accepted by the loan servicer.
Qualification requirements vary by lender and loan type. Documents to review  A copy of the currently recorded deed  The latest mortgage statement  The promissory note or closing documents, if available  Any trust, marital property, or ownership agreement affecting the home  A preliminary title report before a sale or refinance If the deed is unclear, ownership is disputed, or someone is considering adding or removing a name, a California real estate attorney can explain the legal effect before documents are signed.
A lender or loan servicer can explain who is responsible for the debt and what would be required to change the loan.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/should-newlyweds-r.main_text: Comparing Renting and Buying as NewlywedsBuying tends to make more sense when your income, location, savings, and expected time in the area are stable enough to justify the upfront and ongoing costs. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.Compare buying now with waitingBuying sooner may lock in a home that fits the next stage, while waiting can preserve flexibility and give the household more time to build savings or understand its long term needs. Compare the cost of renting with the total cost of owning, including closing costs, maintenance, insurance, taxes, and the possibility of selling sooner than expected.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/should-we-buy-a-ho.main_text: Buying a Home Together Before MarriageGetting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Buying afterward can make sense when your shared budget, savings, location, and expected time in the home support the purchase. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.Build a budget for life after the weddingUse the money actually available after wedding expenses and existing debts. Allow for the down payment, closing costs, moving, repairs, and emergency savings. Agree on a comfortable monthly housing cost before asking a lender to review your borrowing options.Decide how long the home is likely to fitDiscuss work locations, space, family plans, and how long you expect to stay in the area. If a move or job change is likely soon, compare the flexibility of renting with the costs of buying and selling over that shorter period.Agree on ownership and payment responsibilitiesTalk through how each person will contribute, whose income will be used for financing, and how ownership should be recorded. Have the appropriate lender and legal adviser explain the effect of those choices before closing.Compare a real purchase with a real rentalUse homes you could actually buy or rent. Include taxes, insurance, HOA dues, maintenance, and upfront expenses in the comparison. Choose a purchase because it fits your household, rather than because it feels like the next required step after marriage.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

Review those circumstances with an attorney rather than assuming that the wedding date alone settles ownership.The Mortgage ApplicationLenders evaluate an application under the selected loan program and applicable law. life-changes/marriage/should-we-get-a-pr.main_text: Prenuptial Agreements and Buying a Home TogetherA prenuptial agreement can help clarify property and financial expectations before marriage, including a planned home purchase. Whether it is appropriate and enforceable requires advice from qualified attorneys rather than a real estate recommendation.What a prenup can address regarding the houseA prenup can specify how the home would be divided if the marriage ends, including a buyout clause giving one partner the right to purchase the other's share at fair market value, how any difference in down payment contributions should be treated through separate property tracing, and whether the home would be sold or one partner would keep it under specific conditions.Why some couples decide it's unnecessaryBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.When a prenup becomes more importantHow this differs from a cohabitation agreementA prenup is specifically tied to an upcoming marriage and takes effect once the couple marries. A cohabitation agreement serves a similar purpose for unmarried couples and can be used regardless of whether marriage is planned at all, meaning couples who are buying a home together without immediate marriage plans have a comparable legal tool available to them as well.The importance of independent legal counselFor a prenup addressing a home to hold up if challenged later, most states require each partner to have their own attorney, rather than sharing one, and to fully disclose their finances during the process. A prenup signed without independent counsel or full financial disclosure is more vulnerable to being challenged and potentially invalidated during a future divorce.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/should-we-sell-bot.main_text: Combining Households When Both Partners Own HomesYou do not automatically have to sell both homes. Compare each property's equity, mortgage, rental potential, tax consequences and how much cash you need for the next purchase before deciding what to keep or sell.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.Compare buying now with waitingBuying sooner may lock in a home that fits the next stage, while waiting can preserve flexibility and give the household more time to build savings or understand its long term needs. Compare the cost of renting with the total cost of owning, including closing costs, maintenance, insurance, taxes, and the possibility of selling sooner than expected.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/should-you-buy-a-b.main_text: Planning a Home Purchase for a Growing FamilyThink beyond one extra bedroom. Prioritize the space, storage, commute, childcare routine, outdoor needs, and monthly payment that will support your family for the years you expect to stay.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.Choose space for realistic needsEstimate which rooms and features will actually be used during the expected ownership period. Bedrooms, work areas, storage, outdoor space, stairs, school plans, and commute time can matter more than total square footage. Buying extra space too early can increase every ongoing cost, while buying too little may create another move sooner than planned.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/what-happens-to-a-.main_text: Using Equity From a Home Owned Before MarriageIn California, a home owned before marriage generally begins as separate property. That starting point does not settle every later question: changes to title, agreements, and the use of marital funds can affect the analysis. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.Gather the records from before and during marriageKeep the purchase documents, recorded deed, mortgage statements, and records of payments or improvements. These help a lawyer evaluate what happened to the property over time instead of relying on memory or the name on one bill.Separate ownership from the loanReview the deed and mortgage documents separately. A planned title change and a change to who owes the lender are different decisions. Ask the lender what is required for the loan and get legal guidance on the proposed ownership arrangement.Discuss the plan before changing anythingDecide whether the home will remain your shared residence, be rented, or be sold as part of a move. Before transferring title or mixing sale proceeds with other funds, ask a California family law attorney how the proposed steps affect your situation.Then plan the real estate decisionOnce the ownership questions are clear, compare the home’s current value, debt, costs, and suitability for your household. A market estimate helps with the housing plan; it does not determine either spouse’s legal share.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/what-happens-to-th.main_text: Understanding a Shared Home if the Marriage Later EndsIf you divorce later, the house may be kept by one person, sold, or handled another way under the divorce agreement and applicable property law. Buying a home together before or during marriage means thinking ahead to a scenario neither partner wants to imagine, what happens to the house if the marriage ends.How title structure affects the outcomeIf the home was purchased before marriage with both names as joint tenants or tenants in common, that ownership structure typically continues to apply even through a divorce, though divorce proceedings can still address how to handle the shared asset. If the home was purchased during the marriage, it's more commonly treated as marital property subject to division under the state's divorce laws, regardless of whose name is technically on the title.Community property versus equitable distribution statesStates generally fall into one of two categories for dividing marital assets, including a home. Community property states , such as California, Texas, and Arizona typically split marital assets 50/50. Equitable distribution states divide assets in a way considered fair based on the specific circumstances, factors like each spouse's income, contributions, and length of the marriage, which doesn't necessarily mean an even split. Which category a state falls into significantly affects how the home is likely to be handled in a divorce.Why a written agreement matters ahead of timeA cohabitation agreement, made before marriage, or a prenuptial agreement, made in anticipation of marriage, can specify exactly how a jointly purchased home would be handled if the relationship ends, through mechanisms like a buyout right at appraised value or a predetermined equity split, overriding the default state rules that would otherwise apply. This isn't a pessimistic step, it's a practical way to avoid a contentious and expensive legal battle over the home later if circumstances change.What tends to happen without a prior agreementWithout a written agreement in place, resolving what happens to the house typically falls to negotiation between the parties or a family court judge's decision as part of the broader divorce settlement, a process that can take six months to over a year in contested cases and often costs several thousand dollars or more in legal fees, considerably more than having addressed it in writing from the beginning.How courts typically weigh contribution disputesWhen spouses disagree about who contributed more toward a home's down payment or mortgage payments, courts generally require documentation, bank statements, canceled checks, or written records, to substantiate any claim for an uneven split. Verbal recollections alone rarely carry much weight, which is part of why written agreements made at the time of purchase hold up far better than after the fact arguments during a divorce.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/what-if-my-husband.main_text:
Considering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint PurchaseOption 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.
Option 2: Buy a home together. That can mean selling the current home first, or keeping it only if you can comfortably qualify for and manage both properties.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.Ownership and the mortgage are not the sameThe deed identifies ownership, while the promissory note identifies who is responsible for repaying the loan. Adding a spouse to a deed does not add that spouse to the mortgage, and removing a name from title does not release a borrower from the debt. Review the recorded deed and loan documents before planning a sale, refinance, or ownership change.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Understanding a Shared PurchaseBuying together means agreeing on more than a property. Discuss the funds each person contributes, ongoing expenses, use of the home, and how a future change would be handled. A joint mortgage application, the names on title, and a private ownership agreement address different parts of that arrangement.A lender can explain how each borrower’s income, credit, and debts are evaluated. An attorney can review ownership and relationship considerations, including separate property or an unmarried coownership arrangement. Keep documentation of contributions and decisions so the purchase reflects a shared understanding rather than assumptions based only on relationship status.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/what-price-range-c.main_text: Finding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a CoupleStart with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. That gives you a usable price range instead of confusing a lender’s maximum approval with a comfortable budget.Build the decision from the full household pictureCompare the monthly payment, cash needed at closing, savings left afterward, existing debts, current housing costs, and any property either person already owns. Also account for changes that are reasonably expected during the next several years, such as a different commute, children, caregiving, or a need for more space. A lender’s maximum approval is only a borrowing limit; it does not decide what payment will remain comfortable for the household.How joint mortgage qualification worksA couple does not always have to use both incomes or apply jointly. Including another borrower may add income, but it can also add that person’s debts and credit profile. Ask a lender to compare more than one application structure and show the rate, payment, cash required, and qualification result for each. Do not choose a structure based only on the largest approval amount.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.Looking Beyond an Approval AmountA lender evaluates whether a mortgage meets its underwriting requirements, while your household budget also includes expenses that may not appear in that calculation. Consider utilities, transportation, healthcare, childcare, maintenance, and the savings you want to preserve. A payment can meet a lending rule and still feel uncomfortable in daily life.Use current information for the particular property, including taxes, insurance, association dues, and any known repairs. Leave room for changes rather than assuming that every expense will stay fixed. Comparing the full monthly picture and the cash remaining after a move makes it easier to recognize the difference between a qualified purchase and a sustainable one.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/whats-a-good-start.main_text: Choosing a Starter Home as a Newly Married CoupleA good starter home is one you can comfortably afford now and live in long enough to make the purchase worthwhile, without needing it to be your forever home. A starter home doesn't need to be a couple's forever home, but choosing well still requires thinking beyond just the immediate present.Balancing affordability with future flexibilityA practical starter home should fit the household’s ongoing expenses and leave a comfortable reserve. The lender’s maximum approval is not a required spending target, and there is no universal percentage below that amount that suits every couple.Considering resale potentialIf you expect to sell later, consider the home’s layout, condition, maintenance needs, and comparable sales. Balance those practical details with the features and location that work for you now.How much space actually makes senseMany newlyweds choose a two or three bedroom home even without immediate plans for children, since the extra 200 400 square feet of flexible space provides room for a home office, guests, or a growing family down the road, without the higher price point of a larger home purchased before it's genuinely needed.Condos versus single family homes as a starting pointCondos or townhomes are often more affordable entry points for newlyweds in higher cost markets, though they typically come with HOA fees and shared space considerations. A single family home offers more privacy and flexibility for future changes but usually comes at a higher price point for comparable square footage in the same area.Location trade offs worth consideringA starter home slightly farther from a couple's ideal neighborhood, but with a shorter commute or lower price, is often a more financially sound choice than stretching for a dream location before it's genuinely affordable, since a starter home purchased today doesn't need to be in the exact neighborhood a couple ultimately wants to settle in long term.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage/whose-name-should-.main_text: Choosing Home Title for Unmarried BuyersUnmarried buyers can choose a title arrangement that reflects their intended ownership, contributions, and inheritance wishes. The title choice is separate from the mortgage application and should be reviewed with an attorney before the deed is recorded.Joint tenancyJoint tenancy means both partners own the property equally, and it includes what's called a "right of survivorship," if one partner passes away, their share automatically transfers to the surviving partner, without going through probate. This is a common structure for couples who want the simplest possible transfer of ownership if something happens to one of them.Tenants in commonA deed describes ownership, while a mortgage or deed of trust relates to the loan secured by the home. Changing one does not necessarily change the other. Before a transfer, review the recorded ownership documents, outstanding loans, and the authority of each person involved. A name appearing in one document is not a substitute for understanding the complete arrangement.Only one name on the titleSome couples decide only one partner's name goes on the title, often because only one partner qualifies for the mortgage, or because they want to keep the property clearly attributed to one person for financial or family reasons. This leaves the non titled partner with no automatic legal ownership claim, regardless of how much they contribute financially or in other ways, unless a separate written agreement, sometimes called a quitclaim arrangement in reverse or a documented equitable interest agreement, establishes their stake in the property.Why documenting the decision mattersWhichever structure a couple chooses, putting the reasoning and expectations in writing, in a property agreement or cohabitation agreement separate from the deed itself, protects both people if the relationship changes down the road. This is especially true for tenants in common arrangements with unequal ownership shares, where disputes over exact percentages can become complicated without clear documentation from the start.Changing the title structure laterCouples aren't locked into their original choice permanently. Moving from tenants in common to joint tenancy, or vice versa, generally requires recording a new deed, and in some states this can trigger a reassessment of property taxes or transfer tax, so it's worth checking local rules before assuming a title change is a simple, cost free adjustment.California and San Fernando Valley contextFor couples buying or combining homes in California, title, financing, existing property, and household budget may all affect the real estate plan. In the San Fernando Valley, compare those personal factors with current inventory and the long term home features you expect to need.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeCalifornia Courts, Property and Debts in DivorceYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique

life-changes/marriage.html.main_text: MarriageHousing information for couples preparing to buy, own, or combine homes.Moving TimelineChoosing a Home Purchase Timeline Around MarriageThere's no universal right answer to this, since it depends on where a couple is in their relationship, their finances, and how much legal complexity they're comfortable navigating before a wedding takes place.Read MoreHome TitleChoosing Home Title for Unmarried BuyersUnmarried buyers can choose a title arrangement that reflects their intended ownership, contributions, and inheritance wishes. The title choice is separate from the mortgage application and should be reviewed with an attorney before the deed is recorded.Read MoreBuying DecisionManaging Shared Finances Before Buying a Home TogetherYou do not need to merge every account before buying a home together. You do need a clear understanding of purchase contributions, ongoing payments, savings, and the lender’s documentation requirements.Read MoreDivorce PlanningUnderstanding a Shared Home if the Marriage Later EndsIf you divorce later, the house may be kept by one person, sold, or handled another way under the divorce agreement and applicable property law. Buying a home together before or during marriage means thinking ahead to a scenario neither partner wants to imagine, what happens to the house if the marriage ends.Read MoreCredit PlanningJoint Home Buying When Only One Partner Has Strong CreditTwo people may be able to buy together with different credit profiles, but the financing options depend on how the lender evaluates each borrower. A joint application and an application by one borrower can produce different results and different ownership considerations.Read MoreBuying DecisionComparing Buying and Renting While Settling Into Married LifeBuying together may suit a couple with a lasting location plan, suitable financing, and a clear agreement about the home’s responsibilities. Continuing to rent can provide flexibility while work, finances, or shared priorities are still changing.Read MoreAffordabilityHome Buying for Newlyweds With Student Loan DebtNewlyweds can still buy a home with student loan debt by choosing a payment and price range that work after the lender counts the required debt payments. Combining two incomes as a newly married couple can help offset the impact of student loan debt on affordability, but it requires understanding exactly how that debt factors into mortgage qualification.Read MorePrenuptial PlanningPrenuptial Agreements and Buying a Home TogetherA prenuptial agreement can help clarify property and financial expectations before marriage, including a planned home purchase. Whether it is appropriate and enforceable requires advice from qualified attorneys rather than a real estate recommendation.Read MoreBuying TogetherChoosing a Starter Home as a Newly Married CoupleA good starter home is one you can comfortably afford now and live in long enough to make the purchase worthwhile, without needing it to be your forever home. A starter home doesn't need to be a couple's forever home, but choosing well still requires thinking beyond just the immediate present.Read MoreMortgage PlanningJoint Mortgage Qualification for Unmarried BuyersYou do not have to be married to apply for a joint mortgage. Each applicant still needs to meet the lender’s requirements, and a separate ownership agreement can clarify contributions and responsibilities between unmarried buyers.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing a Home Purchase Before and After the WeddingPut both goals on one cash flow plan. Compare the wedding budget, cash needed to buy, emergency savings, and the monthly payment you can handle after the wedding so one goal does not weaken the other.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together When One Spouse Already Has a MortgageA prior mortgage can affect the debt used for qualification and the cash available for the next purchase. A lender can compare the outcome if the existing home is kept, sold, or rented before you make an offer.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying Together With Different Credit Scores or DebtsYou may still be able to buy together. The lender will consider both borrowers’ income, debts, credit, and available cash, so compare joint and single borrower scenarios before deciding how to apply.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Both Spouses’ Incomes for a Home PurchaseMarried couples may use both incomes for a joint mortgage when the lender can document and accept them under the selected program. The lender also reviews debts, credit, assets, and the property, so two incomes do not automatically mean approval.Read MoreLife ChangesChoosing a Home When Combining HouseholdsStart with the people who will live there and the routines the home must support: bedrooms, privacy, work or school needs, storage, transportation, outdoor space, and the monthly cost. A larger home is useful only if it solves the household’s real day to day needs.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing a Starter Home With a Home for a Growing FamilyCompare the cost of moving twice with the cost of buying for the next stage now. The best choice depends on how certain your timing, location, budget, and space needs are, not only on the number of bedrooms.Read MoreLife ChangesUnderstanding Home Title Without Being on the MortgageBeing named on the title generally means you have an ownership interest in the property. Not being named on the mortgage loan generally means you are not one of the borrowers personally responsible for making the loan payments, although the lender’s lien can still affect the property.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering Adding a Spouse to Your Home’s TitleTitle and the mortgage do different things: title reflects ownership, while the mortgage identifies who owes the lender. Do not treat adding a spouse to title as a routine form; understand the ownership, lending, and tax consequences first.Read MoreLife ChangesComparing Renting and Buying as NewlywedsBuying tends to make more sense when your income, location, savings, and expected time in the area are stable enough to justify the upfront and ongoing costs. Compare those costs with a realistic rental alternative before deciding.Read MoreLife ChangesBuying a Home Together Before MarriageGetting married does not create a deadline to buy a house. Buying afterward can make sense when your shared budget, savings, location, and expected time in the home support the purchase. Renting longer is a useful option if those decisions are still unsettled.Read MoreLife ChangesCombining Households When Both Partners Own HomesYou do not automatically have to sell both homes. Compare each property's equity, mortgage, rental potential, tax consequences and how much cash you need for the next purchase before deciding what to keep or sell.Read MoreLife ChangesPlanning a Home Purchase for a Growing FamilyThink beyond one extra bedroom. Prioritize the space, storage, commute, childcare routine, outdoor needs, and monthly payment that will support your family for the years you expect to stay.Read MoreLife ChangesUsing Equity From a Home Owned Before MarriageIn California, a home owned before marriage generally begins as separate property. That starting point does not settle every later question: changes to title, agreements, and the use of marital funds can affect the analysis. Review the history before adding a name, selling, or assuming how the equity belongs to each spouse.Read MoreLife ChangesConsidering a Partner’s Existing Home and a Joint PurchaseOption 1: Live in the home your fiancé already owns. This can be the simpler choice when the home, payment, location, and ownership arrangement work for both of you.Read MoreLife ChangesFinding a Comfortable Home Purchase Range as a CoupleStart with a payment that leaves room for savings, childcare, debt, repairs, taxes, insurance, and everyday life. That gives you a usable price range instead of confusing a lender’s maximum approval with a comfortable budget.Read More

life-changes/relocation/can-a-real-estat.main_text: Understanding Real Estate Support During an Out of State MoveMany parts of a real estate move can be handled remotely, although some legal, lending, inspection, or closing steps may still require your direct involvement. Yes, much of the buying process can be handled remotely with virtual tours, electronic documents and local inspections. You still need a clear financing plan and a trusted local team before making an offer from another state.Plan the move and the real estate transaction togetherWrite out the move date, the date housing is needed in the new area, and the earliest realistic date the current home could be ready to list. Then identify whether money from the current sale is needed for the next purchase. Those dates and cash requirements determine whether selling first, buying first, arranging a coordinated closing, or using temporary housing is realistic.Research daily life before choosing an areaCompare commute patterns at the hours you will travel, housing type, parking, insurance considerations, access to services, and the places you expect to visit regularly. Video tours can narrow the search, but they may not show noise, traffic, grade changes, street activity, or the condition of nearby properties. When possible, test the routine before selecting a home.California and San Fernando Valley contextRelocating into or out of the San Fernando Valley is easier to plan when the sale, purchase, financing, travel, inspections, and moving timeline are treated as one schedule. Local inventory and commute patterns can also make the best neighborhood choice different from what a map suggests.Considering the Destination Before CommittingA relocation combines an employment or personal deadline with a separate housing decision. Compare the destination’s actual commute, property options, insurance, services, and daily expenses before assuming that the move date should also be the purchase date. Temporary housing can provide time to learn the area when important details remain uncertain.Where two properties or multiple professionals are involved, clarify the responsibilities and expected timing for each transaction. Work relocation benefits may also have their own conditions and reimbursement procedures. Keep those requirements separate from the purchase contract so a change in an employer benefit or a home sale does not create an avoidable funding assumption.SourcesConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Buying a HomeConsumer Financial Protection Bureau, Loan EstimatesYour Real Estate PlansWork with Dominique on the real estate part of your situation.Work With Dominique
